lessons.title: Writing Your README
lessons.lessonGoal: Write a complete, professional README documenting your finished capstone project, applying Module 5's documentation principles to your own real, deployed work.

sections.title: Documenting What You Actually Built
sections.content: A README is the document, conventionally named README.md and displayed automatically on a GitHub repository's main page, that explains what a project is, what it does, and how to use or run it — the very first thing most visitors to your repository will actually read, often before they look at any of your actual code. This stage writes a complete, professional README for your now-finished, deployed capstone, applying the same 'write for a reader who lacks your current context' principle Module 5, lesson 7 established for commit messages specifically, now applied at the scale of an entire project rather than one individual change.

sections.title: The Storefront Sign And Description, Not The Inventory Itself
sections.content: Continuing this capstone's storefront metaphor from Module 10, lesson 5: if your deployed site is the actual open storefront, your README is the sign and description posted prominently out front — what's sold here, what makes this particular shop worth stopping at, and basic information about how to find or contact the shop further. A storefront with no sign at all, however well-stocked inside, forces every single passerby to walk in and explore blindly just to figure out what it even is — exactly the friction a missing or poor README creates for anyone (a hiring manager, a fellow developer, your own future self months later) encountering your repository without any other context.

sections.title: A Complete, Professional README Structure
sections.content:
# [Your Name] - Portfolio Website

A brief, one-paragraph description of what this project is and what
it demonstrates.

## Live Site
[https://your-actual-deployed-url.example.com](https://your-actual-deployed-url.example.com)

## Features
- Responsive design (mobile, tablet, desktop)
- [Your Stage 5 interaction, described specifically]
- A working contact form connected to a real backend (or your
  chosen Stage 6 feature, described specifically)

## Built With
- HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS
- Vanilla JavaScript
- Node.js, Express
- [MongoDB / PostgreSQL, if used]

## Running Locally
```
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/your-repo.git
cd your-repo
npm install
npm run dev
```
Requires a `.env` file with: `DATABASE_URL`, `PORT` (see `.env.example`)

## What I Learned
A few genuine sentences about what building this project taught you
or reinforced — specific, not generic.

## Screenshots
[At least one real screenshot of your actual deployed site]

sections.title: Why The 'Running Locally' Section Specifically Matters, Even For A Deployed Project
sections.content: Your project already has a real, live URL (Stage 7) — it's worth understanding precisely why this README still includes instructions for running it locally at all. A README's 'Running Locally' section serves a genuinely different purpose than the live link: it demonstrates, concretely, that you understand and can clearly communicate your own project's actual setup requirements (dependencies, environment variables, the start command), which is exactly the kind of practical knowledge a technical reviewer (unlike a typical visitor just browsing your live site) specifically wants to see demonstrated. This section is also a direct, practical test of whether you've followed Module 10, lesson 6's environment variable guidance correctly: if you genuinely cannot write a clear, accurate 'these are the required environment variables' list, that's a concrete signal your own project's configuration may not be as clean or well-organized as it should be.

sections.title: A Complete, Filled-In README Example, Demonstrating Specificity Over Vagueness
sections.content: This contrasts a vague, generic README excerpt against a specific, genuinely informative one, both describing the same hypothetical project:
sections.code:
<!-- VAGUE - avoid this style -->
## Features
- Nice design
- Some JavaScript
- Backend stuff

## What I Learned
I learned a lot about web development and it was a great experience.


<!-- SPECIFIC - aim for this style instead -->
## Features
- Fully responsive layout using CSS Grid and Tailwind, tested from
  375px mobile widths up through 1440px desktop
- Real-time email validation on the contact form using a regex check
  and live error messaging, with a mobile navigation toggle using
  classList and proper aria-expanded accessibility attributes
- A working contact form that POSTs to an Express backend, validates
  input server-side independently of the frontend, and persists
  submissions to a MongoDB collection

## What I Learned
Building the contact form's backend taught me directly why client-side
validation alone isn't sufficient - I initially skipped server-side
validation entirely, then deliberately tested sending a request directly
via an API client with an empty email field, confirming my own backend
needed its own independent check, exactly as Module 7 had taught.
sections.explanation: The specific version names exact technologies, exact techniques, and exact outcomes — a reader can tell precisely what was actually built and verify those specific claims by visiting the live site or reading the actual code, where the vague version provides no information a reader couldn't have already assumed about literally any portfolio project. The 'What I Learned' section's specific version, in particular, directly demonstrates genuine engagement with this curriculum's actual concepts (Module 7's trust-boundary lesson, concretely applied and tested), which is precisely the kind of evidence a technical reviewer finds far more convincing than a generic, enthusiastic-but-empty statement.

sections.title: How Real README Quality Affects Real Hiring And Collaboration Decisions
sections.content: Real hiring managers and technical reviewers frequently report that a project's README is one of the first things they actually read, and a clear, specific, well-organized README measurably affects their willingness to invest further time exploring a candidate's actual code — directly the same 'write for a reader who lacks your current context' value Module 5, lesson 7 argued for commit messages, now mattering at exactly this higher-stakes moment. Real open-source projects and professional codebases treat README quality as a genuine, often explicitly reviewed deliverable, not an afterthought — a project with excellent code but no meaningful README is frequently undervalued simply because potential users or contributors never get far enough to discover that excellent code in the first place.

sections.title: Common README Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Writing vague, generic descriptions ('a cool website', 'learned a lot') that could describe literally any project, providing no actual information specific to what was genuinely built, exactly this lesson's codeLesson's contrast.

2. Omitting the live deployed URL entirely, or burying it deep in the document rather than placing it prominently near the top, where Module 6, lesson 10's component-thinking-applied-to-information-hierarchy would suggest the most important information should live.

3. Listing 'Running Locally' instructions that don't actually match the real, current setup requirements (a missing environment variable, an outdated command), frustrating anyone who actually tries to follow them.

4. Forgetting to include any actual screenshot or visual reference, leaving a reader without an immediate, low-effort way to see roughly what the project looks like before deciding whether to invest further time exploring it.

5. Writing the README before the project is genuinely finished and deployed, then never updating it to reflect the actual final state — directly the same 'documentation drift' problem real software projects face when documentation isn't kept in sync with an evolving codebase.

sections.title: Documentation As The First, Often Only, Impression
sections.content: This lesson's core argument directly extends Module 5, lesson 7's commit-message philosophy to its logical, highest-stakes conclusion: documentation is frequently the only thing a reader engages with before forming a real opinion about an entire project, making the quality of that documentation disproportionately consequential relative to the relatively modest time it takes to write well. A README written with genuine specificity and care signals the same care likely went into the actual project; a vague, careless README creates doubt about the underlying work's quality even when that work is genuinely solid — documentation quality functions, fairly or not, as a visible proxy for overall project quality in the mind of any reader encountering your work for the first time.

sections.title: Verifying Your README Is Genuinely Complete And Accurate
sections.content: Before moving to Stage 9, hand your README to someone unfamiliar with your project (or imagine doing so honestly) and ask: could they understand what this project is, see it live, and successfully run it locally purely from what's written here, without needing to ask you anything? If any required environment variable, setup step, or genuinely important feature isn't actually mentioned, that's a concrete gap worth fixing now, before a real reviewer in Stage 9 (or beyond) encounters that same gap themselves.

checkpoints.question: Why does this lesson recommend writing specific, concrete descriptions (exact technologies, exact techniques) rather than vague, generic ones in a README?
options: Specific descriptions are required by GitHub's technical specifications
Specific descriptions let a reader verify exact claims and understand precisely what was built, while vague descriptions provide no real information distinguishing the project from any other
Vague descriptions are always shorter and therefore better
This only matters for very large, enterprise-scale projects
checkpoints.explanation: Specific, concrete descriptions let a reader verify and understand exactly what was built, while vague language could describe almost any project and provides little real information.

checkpoints.question: A student's README includes 'Running Locally' instructions, but they list an environment variable that the project no longer actually requires, since it was removed during Stage 6's development. What problem does this create?
options: No problem; minor inaccuracies in documentation never matter
Anyone following these instructions would be misled by inaccurate, outdated information, exactly the kind of documentation drift that undermines a README's usefulness
This is actually required for security reasons
Outdated documentation always improves a project's professional appearance
checkpoints.explanation: Inaccurate, outdated instructions mislead anyone trying to follow them, undermining the README's core purpose of accurately communicating the project's actual current state.

checkpoints.question: According to this lesson, why does README quality matter disproportionately relative to the time it takes to write one well?
options: README quality has no real effect on how a project is perceived
A README is frequently the first, and sometimes only, thing a reader engages with before forming an opinion about an entire project, making its quality a visible proxy for overall project quality
READMEs are only read by automated systems, never by actual people
Writing a good README always takes longer than writing the actual project code
checkpoints.explanation: Since a README is often the first or only thing read before a reader forms an opinion, its quality functions as a visible, disproportionately influential proxy for the perceived quality of the entire project.

lessons.title: Peer Code Review
lessons.lessonGoal: Give and receive genuine code review on real, finished capstone projects, applying Module 5, lesson 5's pull request and review principles for the first time to actual, original work rather than guided examples.

sections.title: Experiencing Review Directly, Not Just Learning About It
sections.content: Module 5, lesson 5 taught pull requests and code review as concepts, with guided, hypothetical examples. This stage is the first point in this entire curriculum where you experience giving and receiving genuine review on real, original, finished work — either your own capstone, or a peer's, or both, depending on this curriculum's actual review-pairing process. The goal is direct, hands-on practice with exactly the skill Module 5, lesson 5 argued is central to real software development: a second perspective catching things the original author, too close to their own work, doesn't notice — now experienced concretely, on a project you (or your peer) genuinely built and care about, rather than a hypothetical example.

sections.title: An Editor Reading Your Manuscript For The First Time, For Real
sections.content: Module 5, lesson 5 compared code review to an editor reading a writer's manuscript before publication. This stage is the actual experience of that editing relationship, not just the comparison: handing your own genuinely finished work to someone else, and receiving their honest, specific feedback — or being the editor yourself, reading someone else's real, completed project for the first time and offering exactly the kind of specific, actionable feedback Module 5, lesson 5 described as the goal of good review. Both directions of this experience — giving review and receiving it — are genuinely valuable and deliberately different skills, each practiced for the first time, for real, in this single stage.

sections.title: A Structured Process For Giving Genuinely Useful Review
sections.content:
When reviewing a peer's capstone, structure your feedback around this curriculum's own recurring frameworks, rather than purely subjective impressions:

1. Structure check (Module 2, Stage 3): Is the HTML semantic? Is the heading hierarchy correct? View the page with styles disabled if your review tool allows it.

2. Styling check (Module 3, Stage 4): Does the layout work responsively across different widths? Is spacing and sizing consistent?

3. Interactivity check (Module 4, Stage 5): Does the JavaScript interaction genuinely work? Try to break it with unexpected input — an empty form, an invalid email, rapid repeated clicks.

4. Backend check (Modules 7-10, Stage 6): Does the backend feature genuinely work on the live site? Is there evidence of server-side validation independent of the frontend (check the Network tab, or ask directly)?

5. Documentation check (Stage 8): Is the README specific and accurate? Could you successfully run this project locally using only the README's own instructions?

For each check, give specific, actionable feedback (Module 5, lesson 5's standard) — not just 'looks good' or 'needs work', but exactly what you checked and what you found.

sections.title: Why Receiving Feedback Well Is Its Own Genuine Skill
sections.content: Module 5, lesson 5 briefly mentioned that taking review feedback personally or defensively undermines review's entire purpose; this stage is where that guidance becomes genuinely, personally relevant for the first time, on work you actually built and likely feel some real ownership over. A specific, well-intentioned critique of your own real project can feel different from an abstract discussion of feedback principles — the actual skill this stage builds is receiving genuinely useful feedback about real, finished work without becoming defensive, recognizing (exactly as Module 5, lesson 5 argued) that the feedback's entire purpose is improving the work, not a judgment of your worth as a developer. Reviewers, in turn, should aim for the same specific, kind, actionable tone Module 5, lesson 5's example pull request descriptions modeled, rather than either empty praise or harsh, non-constructive criticism.

sections.title: Examples Of Specific, Actionable Review Feedback Versus Vague Feedback
sections.content: This contrasts genuinely useful review comments against vague, unhelpful ones, directly applying this stage's structured checklist:
sections.code:
<!-- VAGUE - not genuinely useful to the recipient -->
"The styling looks a bit off."
"The form doesn't really work right."
"Good job overall!"


<!-- SPECIFIC AND ACTIONABLE - genuinely useful -->
"In the Projects section, at exactly 768px width, the grid briefly
shows 2 columns with uneven card heights before snapping to 3 columns
at a slightly wider breakpoint - might be worth checking your
min-width value matches what you intended in your wireframe notes."

"I tried submitting the contact form with an empty email field, and
it submitted successfully anyway - looks like the server-side
validation might not be checking for an empty string specifically,
only for the field being completely absent from the request body."

"Your README's 'Running Locally' section doesn't mention the
DATABASE_URL environment variable, but I got an error until I added
it manually - might be worth adding it to the required variables list."
sections.explanation: Each specific comment names an exact, reproducible observation (a specific width, a specific test input, a specific missing instruction) and, where relevant, a specific hypothesis about the likely cause — giving the recipient enough information to investigate and fix the issue directly, without needing to ask clarifying questions first. This is precisely the standard Module 5, lesson 5's own example pull request descriptions modeled (what changed, why, how to test), now applied to giving review feedback rather than describing a proposed change, but requiring exactly the same underlying discipline of specificity over vague impression.

sections.title: How This Exact Experience Mirrors Real, Ongoing Professional Practice
sections.content: Giving and receiving code review, on real, finished work, by real colleagues, is one of the most frequent, ongoing activities in nearly every professional software development role — this stage is deliberately your first genuine experience with it specifically because it will recur constantly throughout an actual development career, making early, deliberate practice with both giving and receiving it genuinely valuable preparation rather than a one-time capstone formality. Many real engineering teams explicitly train new hires on review etiquette and structured feedback frameworks very similar to this stage's checklist, precisely because review quality (both giving it well and receiving it gracefully) measurably affects how smoothly a team functions and how quickly its members genuinely improve over time.

sections.title: Common Mistakes During Peer Review
sections.content:
1. Giving only vague, low-effort feedback ('looks good', 'needs work') that provides no specific, actionable information the recipient could actually use to improve their project.

2. Reviewing only the visual appearance of a peer's site without actually testing its interactivity (Stage 5) or backend feature (Stage 6) directly, missing exactly the kind of functional gaps this stage's structured checklist is designed to surface.

3. Becoming defensive or dismissive when receiving genuine, specific feedback about your own real project, rather than engaging with it constructively, exactly the mistake Module 5, lesson 5 warned against generally, now personally relevant for the first time.

4. Giving feedback that's harsh or personally critical rather than specific and constructive, focusing on the work's actual gaps rather than implying anything negative about the person who built it.

5. Not actually following the README's own instructions when reviewing a peer's local setup, missing the chance to verify (or disprove) Stage 8's documentation-accuracy requirement directly, exactly the kind of genuine verification this stage's checklist calls for.

sections.title: Review As A Feature Of The Process, Practiced For The First Time For Real
sections.content: Module 5, lesson 5 argued that code review is a feature of how good software actually gets built, not a bureaucratic obstacle — this stage is where that argument stops being something you've merely read about and becomes something you've genuinely experienced, on real work, with real stakes (your own actual capstone, genuinely improved or validated by another person's specific, careful attention). The discipline of giving structured, specific, kind feedback, and of receiving the same gracefully, is a skill that compounds throughout an entire career — every single future code review you give or receive professionally builds on exactly the foundation this one deliberate, guided practice experience is designed to establish.

sections.title: What To Do With The Feedback You Receive
sections.content: Once you've received peer feedback, the appropriate next step is to actually evaluate and, where warranted, act on it — not necessarily implementing every single suggestion uncritically, but genuinely considering each one and either fixing the identified gap or, if you disagree with a specific piece of feedback, being able to articulate clearly why. If your reviewer found a genuine gap (like the missing DATABASE_URL documentation in this lesson's codeLesson example), fixing it before Stage 10's final submission is exactly the kind of responsiveness that demonstrates you've genuinely internalized this stage's purpose, rather than treating review as a purely ceremonial step disconnected from your project's actual final quality.

checkpoints.question: What distinguishes genuinely useful review feedback from vague feedback, according to this lesson?
options: Useful feedback is always longer than vague feedback

Useful feedback names a specific, reproducible observation (an exact width, a specific test input, a specific missing instruction) that gives the recipient enough information to investigate and fix the issue directly
Vague feedback is always kinder and therefore preferable
There is no real difference between specific and vague feedback
checkpoints.explanation: Specific, reproducible feedback gives the recipient enough concrete information to actually investigate and address an issue, unlike vague impressions that provide no actionable detail.

checkpoints.question: A student receives genuine, specific feedback pointing out a real gap in their contact form's server-side validation, and responds by dismissing the feedback without investigating it. What does this represent, based on this lesson's reasoning?
options: An appropriate response, since all feedback should be ignored
Exactly the defensive response Module 5, lesson 5 warned against, undermining review's entire purpose of genuinely improving the work rather than judging the person
This is the correct way to handle all feedback, regardless of its content
Feedback about validation specifically should always be dismissed
checkpoints.explanation: Dismissing genuine, specific feedback without investigation is exactly the defensive response that undermines the constructive purpose of code review, as Module 5, lesson 5 described.

checkpoints.question: What should you do with peer feedback after receiving it, according to this lesson?
options: Implement every single suggestion uncritically, without any independent evaluation
Genuinely evaluate each piece of feedback, fixing identified gaps where warranted or articulating clearly why you disagree, rather than treating review as a purely ceremonial step
Ignore all feedback entirely, since the project is already considered finished
Only respond to feedback that praises the project
checkpoints.explanation: Feedback should be genuinely evaluated and acted upon where warranted, demonstrating real engagement with the review process rather than treating it as a disconnected formality.

lessons.title: Final Submission And Certificate
lessons.lessonGoal: Apply this curriculum's final pre-submission review, submit your complete, deployed, documented, and peer-reviewed capstone, and understand what completing Level 1 genuinely represents.

sections.title: The Final Stage, Not A New Requirement
sections.content: This stage introduces no new building, styling, or feature work — it is the deliberate final review and submission of everything Stages 1 through 9 have already produced: a live, deployed site (Stage 7) with genuine structure (Stage 3), styling (Stage 4), interactivity (Stage 5), and a working backend feature (Stage 6), documented with a specific, accurate README (Stage 8), and improved through genuine peer review (Stage 9). This stage's actual work is a final, holistic verification pass — directly applying Module 10, lesson 10's whole-application production-thinking framework one final time, now to your fully complete, fully reviewed capstone specifically — before formally submitting it and receiving your Level 1 certificate.

sections.title: The Final Walkthrough Before Handing Over The Keys
sections.content: Continuing this capstone's construction metaphor through its final stage: every prior stage built, finished, connected, and had inspected one part of the building — this stage is the final, complete walkthrough a contractor performs before formally handing the finished building's keys over to its owner. Every system gets checked one last time, together, as a whole: does the front door (your live URL) actually open, do the lights (your interactivity) actually work, does the plumbing (your backend feature) actually function, is the building's documentation (your README) accurate and complete. This isn't redundant with earlier inspections — it's the final, holistic confirmation that everything checked individually across nine separate stages genuinely works together, as one complete, finished whole, before formally declaring the project done.

sections.title: The Final Pre-Submission Checklist
sections.content:
Before submitting, confirm every item below, directly against your own actual, live project:

1. Live and reachable: your real URL from Stage 7 loads correctly, right now, in a fresh browser session
2. Complete content: every section from your Stage 2 plan is genuinely present (Hero, About, Projects with 2-3 real projects, Contact, Footer)
3. Responsive: your site works correctly across mobile, tablet, and desktop widths, with no broken layouts or horizontal scrolling
4. Genuinely interactive: your Stage 5 feature works correctly, including under the adversarial testing (invalid input, repeated actions) that lesson recommended
5. Backend genuinely connected: your Stage 6 feature works on the LIVE site specifically (not just locally), with server-side validation independently verified
6. Accurate documentation: your README (Stage 8) is specific, accurate, and includes your real live URL prominently
7. Peer review addressed: at least one genuine finding from Stage 9's review has been considered and, where warranted, fixed
8. Clean Git history: your repository reflects a genuine, well-tracked progression through these stages (Module 5's commit discipline), not one single enormous final commit

sections.title: Why This Final Checklist Is A Genuine Gate, Not A Formality
sections.content: This checklist deliberately requires re-verifying items that earlier stages already individually confirmed (responsiveness in Stage 4, interactivity in Stage 5, the backend connection in Stage 6) specifically because Module 10, lesson 7's full stack debugging lesson and lesson 10's production-thinking lesson both established that individually-correct pieces don't automatically guarantee a correct, connected whole — a change made during Stage 9's review response, for instance, could plausibly have introduced a new gap in something that worked correctly before that specific fix. This final, holistic re-check is the genuine, practical payoff of this curriculum's repeated argument that verification should happen at the level of the complete, connected system, not only at the level of each individual piece checked once, in isolation, and never revisited.

Item 7 specifically demonstrates Stage 9's review genuinely being acted upon, not merely received and set aside, closing the loop this capstone's entire 9-stage sequence has been building toward.

sections.title: What Completing This Capstone, And Level 1 Overall, Genuinely Represents
sections.content: Completing this capstone means you have personally taken a project from a blank plan through genuine, live deployment, with real interactivity, a real backend connection, real documentation, and real peer feedback incorporated — the complete, authentic lifecycle of a genuine software project, practiced once, deliberately, under guidance, specifically so you can repeat this same lifecycle independently and confidently on every future project throughout your actual career. This also marks the completion of this curriculum's entire Level 1: Foundations, spanning HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Git, React, backend development, databases, authentication, full stack connection, and now this capstone's genuine, independent application of all of it together — a foundation Level 2's more advanced, intermediate-level content will build directly upon.

sections.title: Common Mistakes At This Final Stage
sections.content:
1. Treating this final checklist as a formality to rush through, rather than genuinely, individually re-verifying each item directly against the live project, exactly as this lesson's codeLesson example demonstrated doing honestly.

2. Submitting without actually addressing any of Stage 9's peer review findings, treating that entire stage as disconnected from the project's actual final state rather than genuinely incorporating its feedback.

3. Discovering a genuine gap during this final review (a broken live link, an outdated README) and submitting anyway without fixing it, rather than treating this checklist as a genuine gate that should block submission until items are actually resolved.

4. Comparing your own capstone unfavorably against an imagined, idealized 'perfect' version rather than honestly evaluating it against this capstone's actual, stated requirements from Stage 1 — a complete, working, appropriately-scoped project that meets every genuine requirement is a legitimate, complete success, not a lesser achievement than an unnecessarily more elaborate one.

5. Rushing through Level 1's conclusion without taking a moment to genuinely recognize the actual scope of what's been completed — ten full modules, eight closing 'thinking' lessons, and now one complete, independently-built, genuinely deployed capstone project.

sections.title: Fundamentals Are Still The Real Curriculum, One Final Time, At The Scale Of A Real Project
sections.content: This lesson is the ninth and final time Level 1 explicitly names this recurring theme (after Modules 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10), and it does so at the largest possible scale this level offers: not one concept, one feature, or even one module, but one entire, real, independently-completed project, built and verified using the combined judgment from every single prior closing lesson at once. The specific tools used throughout this capstone — HTML, CSS, Tailwind, vanilla JavaScript, Express, a database, deployment platforms — will inevitably evolve or be replaced over an actual career; the underlying discipline this capstone deliberately practiced — plan before building, verify each layer before building on it, validate trust boundaries, debug systematically, document honestly, receive feedback gracefully, and verify the complete whole before calling anything finished — is what genuinely transfers to every future project, in any technology, for the rest of a real development career.

sections.title: What To Do If Your Final Checklist Reveals A Genuine Gap
sections.content: If this stage's final checklist reveals a genuine, real gap — a broken live link, an interactive feature that fails under adversarial testing, an inaccurate README — the correct response is to actually fix it before submitting, exactly as this lesson's failureCases section described, applying whichever specific module's lesson the gap actually belongs to (Module 10, lesson 7's debugging sequence remains the right general-purpose tool for tracing any gap to its actual layer and cause). Discovering and fixing a genuine gap during this final, deliberate review is not a failure of the process — it is the process working exactly as intended, precisely the same way Module 10, lesson 10's own deployment example found and fixed two genuine gaps specifically because that lesson's systematic review was actually applied honestly, rather than skipped or rushed.

checkpoints.question: A student's final checklist reveals that their live site's backend feature, which worked correctly during Stage 6, no longer works after a Stage 9 review-response fix. What is the correct response, according to this lesson?
options: Submit anyway, since the feature worked correctly at some earlier point

checkpoints.explanation: Discovering and fixing a genuine gap during final review is the process working as intended; the correct response is to fix it before submission, not to submit with a known, unresolved gap.

options: Only the exact specific technologies used (HTML, CSS, Express, etc.), since tools never change
